title: Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis
hookLine: a movement in white clothes, reciting the Name and boycotting British goods

lines: NO BRITISH POST, COURTS OR CLOTH.
cards: White cloth. That's what you'd notice first. A crowd gathers in a village in the Punjab, everyone in plain white, turbans tied straight across the forehead.
They're reciting the Name together. Some, caught up in it, cry out loud, and the neighbors start calling them Kukas, from those cries.
Their leader asks something bold for the time: don't use the British post, don't go to British courts, don't wear foreign cloth. The leader is Baba Ram Singh.

teach.h: NAMDHARI — ONE WHO HOLDS THE NAME.
teach.b: First, the word. Namdhari is the name the movement chose for itself, and its followers understand it as one who holds the Name. Kuka was the neighbors' nickname, tied, the story goes, to the cries during their recitation.
Second, the teacher. Baba Ram Singh came from the village of Bhaini, in the Ludhiana district, and had served as a soldier before he turned to teaching.
He called people to the Name, to the Khalsa's discipline, and to plain living: white clothes, no meat, no alcohol, honest work.
He spoke against the dowry and against killing baby daughters, and held simple weddings, sometimes for many couples at once, without heavy cost. Third, the refusal.

teach.h: NO BRITISH COURTS, POST OR CLOTH.
teach.b: Under British rule, he told his followers to stay away from British schools, courts, post and goods. Settle disputes among yourselves. Weave your own cloth.
Some historians see in this an early form of the boycotts of India's later freedom movement. The British watched him closely. Fourth, a fair word on difference.
Namdharis hold that the line of living Gurus continued after Guru Gobind Singh, through Baba Balak Singh and Baba Ram Singh.
The Akal Takht and the wider Khalsa Panth hold that Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib, and that no person holds it after him.
This lesson tells his story, and leaves that question to each community.
A simple rule, kept firmly, can say more than a long argument.

how: Namdhari Sikhs wear white, tie their turbans straight across the forehead, recite the Name together, and remember Baba Ram Singh as a teacher of plain living and of refusing British goods and courts.

o: one who was named by a Guru
one who keeps the Name secret

Baba Ram Singh told followers to avoid British courts, post and goods

games.q: you follow Baba Ram Singh, and a neighbor wrongs you. where do you take the dispute?
o: to the British court in town.
to your own community to settle.
games.why: Baba Ram Singh asked his followers to stay out of British courts and settle disputes among themselves.

practice: Notice what you're wearing right now, not to judge it, just the color, the weight, whether it's simple or busy, then let your attention move from the cloth to the breath underneath it.
Ask one quiet question: what's one plain, firm thing I could keep without explaining it to anyone? If you pray, repeat Waheguru on each breath, as the Namdharis recite the Name.

wordCard.voice: Namdhari. One who holds the Name; the followers of Baba Ram Singh, dressed in white, also nicknamed Kukas. Today's word.

orig.note: Namdhari, one who holds the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: simple and firm. White cloth, a straight turban, a rule that doesn't bend. See you tomorrow.
